description: A modular, stack-agnostic toolkit for AI coding agents to autonomously find, reproduce, and patch vulnerabilities.

written.description: Reads a codebase and its commit history, builds a threat model from them, and sends agents to chase each hypothesis it raises. It then tries to reproduce each finding in a sandbox and attacks its own patch to check the fix holds, working from source alone with no running target.

alive.last_commit_message:
feat(reproduce): a harness observes the sink; it never alters it

The live run on the research target reproduced a tar-slip whose payload
the guest's Python had already stopped: tarfile's default extraction
filter raised OutsideDestinationError. The retry monkeypatched
TarFile.extractall to pass filter="fully_trusted", wrote the sentinel
from inside that hook whenever a member name held "..", and the gate
accepted it. The finding went out as an arbitrary file write that was
"verified by file creation outside the staging directory", which never
happened on that runtime.

Nothing in the reproducer prompt or the skill said what a hook may do.
Both now say it, in the same words: prefer evidence the payload itself
produces at the sink; a hook or wrapper is a last resort for effects the
sandbox cannot show, and may only observe -- same arguments through to
the original, sentinel written on the condition that the attacker value
arrived -- never changing the sink's arguments, defaults, filters,
environment, permissions or exception handling. And a safeguard in the
runtime or a library that stops the payload is a result, recorded as
failed_repro / failed_to_reproduce citing "Mitigated by runtime:
<safeguard> (<component and version>)", so the report says
exploitability depends on the deployed version; it is not disabled or
downgraded to make the payload land.

Prompt and skill only; the deterministic side (detecting a sink that was
rebound by the PoC) is separate work.
